Independent confirmation of this, observed live on 2026-07-29 — five weeks after this issue was opened, on a separate deployment. Adding field evidence plus two details I don't think are captured above.

  ## The gate survived the reactions.go refactor

  This issue cites the blanket entry gate at `reactions.go:65`. That code has since been restructured into the queue-every-applicable-nudge reducer (good — it fixed the separate bug where a CI failure suppressed review feedback on the same PR). **But the needs-input
  gate survived the refactor.** At current HEAD:

  ```go
  // reactions.go:564
  func cannotNudge(rec domain.SessionRecord) bool {
        return rec.IsTerminated || rec.Activity.State.NeedsInput() || rec.Activity.State == domain.ActivityExited
  }
  ```

  `cannotNudge(rec)` is called at `reactions.go:172` — the top of the very function that queues the merge-conflict nudge at `:221-236`. So a session in a needs-input state still returns before the conflict nudge is ever queued. The refactor moved the gate; it didn't
  lift the conflict path above it.

  Worth noting the defect has now persisted across a full implementation change. We are running `@aoagents/ao` 0.9.4 (the pre-Go TypeScript implementation), where the same path is closed by a *different* mechanism — `maybeDispatchMergeConflicts` in
  `ao-core/dist/lifecycle-manager.js:2004-2009` gates on a six-value status allowlist (`pr_open`, `ci_failed`, `review_pending`, `changes_requested`, `approved`, `mergeable`) that simply omits the parked state. Two different implementations, two different mechanisms,
  same closed path — which suggests it needs a deliberate fix rather than one that happens incidentally during restructuring.

  In our version the intended contract was documented directly above the guard, and the guard contradicts it:

  ```js
  /**
   * Dispatch merge conflict notifications to the agent session.
   * Conflicts are detected from the PR enrichment cache or getMergeability()
   * and dispatched independently of the session status (conflicts can coexist
   * with ci_failed, changes_requested, etc.).
   */
  ```

  "dispatched independently of the session status" — followed twenty lines later by a status allowlist.

  ## The escalation timer never arms either

  This is the part that makes it fully silent rather than merely quiet. The `merge-conflicts` reaction ships with `escalateAfter: "15m"`:

  ```
  "merge-conflicts": { auto: true, action: "send-to-agent",
    message: "Your branch has merge conflicts. Rebase on the default branch and resolve them.",
    escalateAfter: "15m" }
  ```

  That timer only starts **after** a dispatch. No dispatch means no escalation — so the human doesn't get a late notification either. The failure isn't "the agent wasn't nudged, but someone gets told eventually"; it's that every notification path downstream of the
  dispatch is dead too. That may be worth folding into the fix criteria alongside the three surfacing paths already listed.

  ## Field evidence, with a positive control

  Live sequence on our deployment:

  - PR A merged at `14:18:11Z` and conflicted PR B, owned by a session parked awaiting operator input (it had transitioned into that state at `02:07:46Z`).
  - GitHub reported `mergeable = CONFLICTING`, `mergeStateStatus = DIRTY` on PR B.
  - ~40 minutes later: no agent nudge, no operator notification, nothing.
  - Zero activity-events rows for that session after `14:18`.
  - Across the entire activity-events database, exactly **one** conflict-related event has ever been recorded, for any session.

  That one event is the useful part — it's a **positive control**. A different session on the *same daemon* with the *same config* received `reaction.action_succeeded | send-to-agent merge-conflicts` at `2026-07-29T01:18:18.406Z`, while it was in an eligible state. So
  the reaction config, the watcher, and the delivery path are all live and working. The session's activity state is the only variable that closes the path — which rules out config drift, a dead pane, or a delivery failure as explanations.

  One corroborating detail on how invisible this is: the parked session's stored `lifecycle.pr.lastObservedAt` was ~13 hours stale by the time the conflict arrived.

  ## Reproduction

  1. Give a session an open PR and let it park awaiting operator input.
  2. Merge something from another branch that conflicts with that PR.
  3. Wait through several full poll cycles.

 Observed: no merge-conflict nudge, no escalation after 15 minutes, nothing in activity events. Repeat with the session in an eligible state instead and the nudge fires.

 Happy to supply anything more from our side if it helps. We've had to add a status-agnostic external poller against the GitHub REST API as a stopgap, since we can't rely on AO surfacing this.

**Post-merge notes on the telemetry split**

The two-layer drop is the right shape, and the part most likely to have been subtly wrong is correct: `ao hooks` is a single cobra command with two positional args, so `CommandPath()` returns exactly `ao hooks` and the equality check matches. Dropping before the reservoir reservation is also a good call, since blocked commands no longer consume dedup slots.

I built the daemon and pointed `AO_TELEMETRY_POSTHOG_HOST` at a local capture endpoint to observe what actually goes on the wire. Five real `ao hooks claude-code post-tool-use` invocations produced zero events, and `ao status`, `ao project ls`, `ao session ls`, `ao orchestrator ls` were all silent. A control run of `ao version` exported correctly as `ao.v2.cli.invoked` with `legacy_event_name: ao.cli.invoked` and `telemetry_schema_version: 2`, and with `AO_SESSION_ID` unset it also refreshed `ao.v2.app.active` on `channel: cli`. The rename and the drop both work for current clients.

Four things worth following up.

**`docs/telemetry.md` now asserts a state the code does not implement.** The change flips "session recording is enabled for the renderer" to "session recording is disabled by default", but `buildPostHogConfig` is untouched and sets no `disable_session_recording`, while `telemetry.ts` imports `posthog-js/dist/module.full.no-external`, the bundle carrying the replay recorder. Recording remains client-enabled and gated only on the project-side toggle. Root `README.md` was not updated either, so it still says recording is enabled, and the two docs now contradict each other. Replay bills per recording rather than per event, so it sits outside every limiter in `telemetry.ts` and is the one line item that can grow independently of event volume. Either set `disable_session_recording: true` or revert the doc line.

**The "10x+ immediately" estimate is not something this change delivers.** The 962,837 weekly `ao hooks` events come from already-deployed clients, and nothing in the diff reduces their volume. The reduction depends entirely on ingestion drop rules configured in the PostHog UI, which have no representation in the repo, so there is no way to tell from the code whether they were ever enabled. Reading the merge, it looks like the spend problem is closed. Suggest separating what shipped from what still requires manual PostHog configuration, and filing a tracking issue for the latter, otherwise the runbook's estimate reads as a result.

**`isRoutineInternalCLICommand` is duplicated verbatim in `backend/internal/cli/root.go` and `backend/internal/httpd/router.go` with nothing asserting the two lists agree.** Divergence is silent in both directions: adding a command only to the CLI list leaves old clients leaking it, and adding it only to the daemon list drops a command the CLI still counts. Given the deliberate no-import boundary between the two packages, a small shared list would be safer than a copy.

**The gate is stricter than the threat it defends against.** Posting variant command paths to `/internal/telemetry/cli-invoked` as an old or foreign client would, three of six got through: `"ao  hooks"` with a double space, `"AO HOOKS"`, and `"ao hooks claude-code post-tool-use"`. They were then classified `actor_type: user` and so counted as active-user signal, with `command_path` arriving hashed as `sha256:...`. No real client produces those forms and the endpoint is loopback-only, so this is not current volume, but the daemon-side gate exists specifically for clients you do not control. The first two close with a one-line change in both copies:

```go
switch strings.ToLower(strings.Join(strings.Fields(commandPath), " ")) {
```

Related: `cliActorType` falls through to `user` for any unrecognized path, so an unknown command is DAU-eligible by default. For a cost-control change, a conservative fallback would fit better.

**Minor:** the rewrite of `TestCLIInvokedRouteSeparatesAgentAndSystemInvocationsFromActiveUsers` dropped the only coverage of the `"ao hooks" -> "agent"` inference in `cliActorType`. That branch is now unreachable in effect, since `isRoutineInternalCLICommand` returns first, and no test would fail if it were removed.

Three things below, one of which I would fix before merge.

## 1. The `cliActorType` user allowlist enumerates leaf command names, not command paths

The list contains 17 entries that are not real command paths: `ao add`, `ao merge`, `ao kill`, `ao rename`, `ao claim-pr`, `ao cancel`, `ao submit`, `ao trigger`, `ao restore`, `ao cleanup`, `ao clear`, `ao delete`, `ao remove`, `ao restart`, `ao launch`, `ao resolve-comments`, `ao import-projects`. Those are the leaf names of `ao project add`, `ao pr merge`, `ao session kill`, `ao review cancel` and so on.

The consequence is the inverse: real paths are missing, and since the default is now `system`, they emit nothing at all. I enumerated the command tree and ran `cliActorType("", path)` for every path on this branch. 46 real paths classify as `system`, including all 28 `ao browser *` commands, `ao pr merge`, `ao preview start|stop|status|clear`, `ao review ls|cancel|trigger`, `ao session claim-pr`, `ao agent ls`, `ao dev`, and `ao orchestrator done`.

Most of that is latent, since current CLIs always populate `actor_type` and short-circuit before the allowlist, and `ao browser` postdates actor stamping (#2947, 2026-07-27) so it can never arrive actor-less. But some of it is live. Querying actor-less CLI events in the current billing period for paths the allowlist does not cover:

| command_path | events | installs |
|---|---:|---:|
| `ao agent ls` | 639 | 98 |
| `ao session claim-pr` | 392 | 29 |
| `ao smoke set` | 264 | 1 |
| `ao project orchestration get` | 46 | 3 |
| `ao project orchestration set` | 44 | 3 |
| `ao dev import-projects` | 37 | 11 |
| `ao handoff` | 33 | 5 |
| `ao smoke list` | 30 | 1 |

`ao agent ls` across 98 installs stops producing telemetry and stops contributing CLI-channel DAU. Modest in volume, but it is silent: a `system` classification emits nothing, so nothing surfaces when the list drifts.

Rather than curating the list by hand, consider a test that walks `NewRootCommand(Deps{}).Commands()` recursively and asserts every `CommandPath()` classifies as something other than `system` unless it is in an explicit named exception set. That would have caught the leaf-name mistake and prevents the list rotting as commands are added.

## 2. The updated DAU query in `docs/posthog-cost-controls.md` does not run

Run against project 475752 it fails with:

```
No scope or CTE available
Tables referenced: events
```

The `WITH <expression> AS normalized_command_path` sits before the `SELECT`, so `properties.command_path` has no table scope to resolve against. Moving the expression into a subquery works. This version returns 40 rows against the real project:

```sql
SELECT day, uniqExact(distinct_id) AS active_installs FROM (
  SELECT distinct_id, toDate(timestamp) AS day,
    lower(trim(replaceRegexpAll(toString(properties.command_path), '\s+', ' '))) AS ncp,
    properties.channel AS channel, properties.actor_type AS actor
  FROM events
  WHERE timestamp >= now() - INTERVAL 90 DAY AND event = 'ao.app.active')
WHERE NOT (
  channel = 'cli' AND (actor IS NULL OR actor = '')
  AND (ncp IN ('ao hooks','ao session ls','ao session get','ao orchestrator ls',
               'ao status','ao project ls','ao project get','ao pty-host')
       OR startsWith(ncp, 'ao hooks ') OR startsWith(ncp, 'ao pty-host ')))
GROUP BY day ORDER BY day DESC
```

## 3. The documented normalization does not match the Go implementation

`trim` runs before the whitespace collapse, so whitespace that is not a literal space survives as a trailing space:

```sql
SELECT lower(replaceRegexpAll(trim(BOTH ' ' FROM 'ao  hooks\t'), '\s+', ' ')),  -- 'ao hooks ' (doc)
       lower(trim(replaceRegexpAll('ao  hooks\t', '\s+', ' ')))                 -- 'ao hooks'  (matches Go)
```

`strings.Fields` in `NormalizeCommandPath` produces `ao hooks`, so the two definitions disagree despite the doc claiming "lowercase with whitespace collapsed". It happens to be masked here because every routine path also has a `startsWith(..., '<path> ')` clause that catches the trailing-space form. Worth swapping the order so the SQL and the Go agree, since the doc is the reference for anyone writing the ingestion rule by hand.

## Notes, not blockers

They fail identically on `origin/main`, with and without `AO_*` environment variables set, so this is pre-existing rather than introduced here. Separately, one actor-less `command_path` in the data reads `Nyrokme-Agency-Service hooks`, alongside earlier events named `moly-engine.onboarding.*` and `to.onboarding.*`. Those look like rebranded forks still shipping the bundled project key, which means any command-based ingestion rule keyed on the literal `ao hooks` will not match their hook traffic. Out of scope for this PR, but relevant to how the cost-control predicate is written.

Field evidence in support of this, from running a large fleet of worker sessions.

At one moment on a single host, 9 non-terminated sessions were sitting idle. 8 had signalled at least once (they had run and finished a turn); 1 had **never** signalled — no first signal was ever recorded — and had been idle for 26.47 hours. All 9 carried the identical persisted activity state, so today they render the identical grey sidebar dot. The daemon already holds the fact that separates them (whether a first signal ever arrived); the dot just never reads it.

The operator cost is exactly what this PR targets: the one view used to answer "what is actually running" cannot distinguish a session that is simply awaiting its next message from one that never started at all. At fleet scale, genuinely stuck sessions get missed in the grey.

One question this raised for us: does keying the dot on the attention zone also separate a never-signalled session from one that finished a turn cleanly? Tracing the diff, it does — the daemon derives `no_signal` for the never-started case and `idle` for the finished-turn case, and `attentionZone` routes `no_signal` to the action (needs-you) zone while `idle` stays in the working zone, so the two now render as different dots (past the 90s no-signal grace, which our 26h case clears comfortably). The `no_signal` row in the new table test pins exactly this. So from our side that case looks covered — sharing the never-started data point as a concrete example rather than a gap.

ran this locally in the desktop app. the file diff side works nicely, but the browser panel was stretching the page and squeezing its toolbar controls on both maximize and restore. pushed two commits to the branch.

### browser resize (59b5d019f)

root cause is that `.browser-panel` is the Flip target and `scale: false` tweens its real width/height, so every frame is a genuine relayout of the panel's contents. the toolbar is a dense single row, 8 icon buttons plus a `flex-1` URL field, and at docked width those controls are already near their floor, so tweening through that range visibly squeezes and re-spaces them. the snapshot compounds it: at `object-fit: contain` its 100%/100% box changes aspect every frame, so the captured page rescales continuously and grows letterbox bands against `--bg`.

the files view escapes this because it's a vertical list, so reflowing its width just re-wraps text. that's why only one of the two surfaces looks wrong.

rather than try to animate the chrome nicely, the panel now sits the tween out. `useFlipTransition` stamps `data-flipping` on the target for exactly the tween's duration, and the panel's CSS uses that to hide the toolbar and let the viewport fill the whole box, so the growing or shrinking window reveals and clips one static image and nothing reshapes. toolbar fades back in as it lands. snapshot moves to `object-fit: cover` for the popout case, which is full-bleed and uniformly scaled, cropping instead of letterboxing, so it reads as a zoom. tab-switch keeps `contain` since its box shape doesn't change.

the mark is cleared on complete, on interrupt, and on unmount. worth calling out that `kill()` never fires `onComplete`, so without the interrupt path an abandoned node would stay marked and the panel would be permanently chrome-less.

i also corrected the comment above the hook. it said real layout tweening means "nothing but the intended box ever changes shape", which is the assumption the approach was built on and is exactly what breaks here.

### two review items (76dfb1da5)

**the description says this adds `--duration-emphasized`/`--ease-emphasized` tokens, but those don't exist.** `grep -rn emphasized` over the repo returns nothing. the values are hardcoded in `useFlipTransition.ts` as `DEFAULT_DURATION_MS = 320` and `DEFAULT_EASE = "expo.out"`, and DESIGN.md documents them as prose. i added the tokens for real in `tokens.css` and the hook now reads the duration from the document root, with the documented default as fallback. the ease stays a GSAP ease since that's what drives the tween, and `--ease-emphasized` is its cubic-bezier equivalent for the CSS-driven parts.

**the files view mounts twice while maximized.** `SessionView` passes the same `filesMaximize.setNodeRef` to both the rail's `SessionFilesView` and the full-window overlay, and `handleToggleFilesPopOut` forces the inspector to the files tab, so both are mounted at once and both claim that one ref. whichever attaches last silently wins. on restore the overlay unmounts and hands back `null` while the docked one stays mounted, so the animation falls through to an immediate settle. it only works today because `SessionFilesView` uses an inline arrow for `ref`, which React re-attaches every render. that's accidental rather than designed.

`BrowserView` already guards against exactly this (`SessionInspector.tsx`, "must not mount a second BrowserPanelView"). the files tab now does the same and offers a Return to panel action.

### what's good

the `releasing` crossfade is a real race fix and the reasoning holds up, `measureAndSend()`'s IPC round trip and the React state update do land on different ticks. clearing `popoutTransitionRef` on session switch is a genuine catch and it's tested. `inert` plus the grid-row collapse is the right way to keep the diff row mounted. the comments explain why rather than restating the code, which is rarer than it should be.

### verification

`tsc --noEmit` clean, 897/897 renderer tests pass. added tests for the `data-flipping` lifecycle, the duration token, and the files guard, and mutation-tested four of them: breaking the interrupt cleanup, the settle cleanup, the token read, and the files guard each fail a test.

the unchecked manual-verification box in the test plan was the right call to flag. this is what a click-through catches. worth another pass on your side once you pull, particularly whether the toolbar drop-out reads as too abrupt, since the fade-in duration is the knob there.

follow-up, and a correction to my earlier comment: **the browser panel no longer animates its maximize at all.** the approach I described above (`data-flipping`, hiding the toolbar, `object-fit: cover`) is gone. if you read that comment, skip its browser-transition section, the review findings below it still stand.

### why it was removed

I kept fixing artifacts one at a time and each fix exposed the next one:

1. the toolbar squeezed through the tween, since `scale: false` moves real width/height and the toolbar is a dense row already near its floor at docked width
2. fixed that by hiding it, then the page visibly zoomed in and snapped back at the handoff, because the frozen frame was being fitted to a box that resizes for the whole transition while the live view always renders at 1x
3. fixed that by pinning the frame at 1x, and then the panel just grew into empty space, which looked worse than either

underneath all three, the tween relayouts the whole panel subtree every frame for 320ms, which is what actually read as lag. none of my fixes touched that.

the real constraint is structural: browser content is a native `WebContentsView` that Chromium composites above the page. it cannot be transformed, clipped or tweened. so any grow/shrink is a captured bitmap standing in for the page, and a bitmap can't agree with a live view that relayouts at the new size. scale it and it zooms; pin it and you get blank space. there's no version of this that's both smooth and honest without solving the native-view problem first.

so maximize is now an immediate swap. the frozen frame stays, but only for what it's genuinely good at, covering the native view's handoff, which is an IPC round trip that would otherwise flash, and it crossfades out once the live view is up at the new bounds. nothing tweens layout, so there's nothing to lag.

## Alternative/likely cause found: external cleanup script sending SIGTERM to long-running agent processes

Update on my "orchestrator worktree disappears" observation above — the trigger may not be internal to AO at all.

I have a local convenience script (not part of AO) that kills long-idle background processes matching certain command patterns (`app-server-broker`, `cline-host`, `context7-mcp`, `SkyComputerUseClient`) older than a configurable age threshold (default 60 min), to reclaim RAM/swap. It sends `SIGTERM` (not `SIGKILL`) and does NOT touch the filesystem directly — no `rm`, no `git worktree remove` calls.

However, on 2026-08-01 I ran it with `--apply` against ~470 matching processes, and shortly after, a `direct-cli` orchestrator worktree ended up in a broken state (directory recreated via a fresh `git clone`, ~25 min after the cleanup ran). The orchestrator session in the AO DB still showed `activity_state=idle, is_terminated=0`, and tmux stayed attached — the same signature as the original report.

**Working theory:** if an agent process bound to that orchestrator's worktree was mid-flight on a git operation when it received SIGTERM, it could be interrupted mid-operation and leave the directory in a half-torn-down state. Someone/something then likely deleted the remnants and re-cloned, consistent with the timeline, though I don't have a captured stack trace or log proving the exact sequence — daemon logs weren't being persisted at the time (a separate, already-known gap: the app-owned daemon only redirects stdout/stderr to a log file when a keep-alive env flag is set; under normal GUI launch it doesn't).

This doesn't rule out an AO-internal cause for the original occurrence (no external cleanup was involved there, as far as I can tell), but it's a plausible explanation for at least this recurrence, and worth ruling in/out separately from AO's own teardown logic. Flagging it in case others run similar "reap idle helper processes" tooling alongside AO — long-running agent/worker processes inside an AO-managed worktree can look "idle" by CPU/age heuristics while actually mid-operation.

### 1. The differential path is off on macOS

PR #3151 (`fix(release): skip blockmap sidecar for macOS zips`, merged 2026-07-29) stops emitting the `.blockmap` sidecar for darwin zips, so `electron-updater` has nothing to drive a differential download with and always fetches the full zip. That removes the reconstruction step this issue's root-cause hypothesis pointed at.

### 2. The already-published sidecars are gone

Re-verified just now across the 60 most recent releases: **0** mac/darwin `.blockmap` assets remain. The 90 sidecars still live are all platforms where the differential path is intended (45 `.AppImage.blockmap`, 45 `.exe.blockmap`). So no client can pick up a stale mac sidecar from an older release either.

### 3. A real end-to-end update run passes

Ran the macOS update e2e ([run 30758538690](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/actions/runs/30758538690)) on a real `macos-latest` Apple silicon host against the real published feed, not a fixture:

- **baseline:** `v0.11.2-nightly.202607301613` installed into `/Applications`, verified codesigned, notarized and stapled
- **target:** `0.11.2-nightly.202608021445` resolved through the live `nightly-mac.yml`
- **result:** `PASS: 0.11.2-nightly.202607301613 updated to 0.11.2-nightly.202608021445, relaunched, daemon alive`

That covers the exact step that failed here: the update downloaded, Squirrel staged it, ShipIt performed the `ditto` swap on quit, and the relaunched bundle both reported the new version from its `Info.plist` and answered on the daemon's loopback `/healthz`. The post-update `codesign --verify --deep --strict` / `spctl` / `stapler validate` trio also passed on what ShipIt actually left on disk, so the seal survives the swap. No `ditto: No such file or directory` errors.

**Wall clock: 1m 19s** measured by the job's own instrumentation (79s), 90s for the whole job including checkout and setup.

Both baseline and target were published after #3151, so neither carries a mac blockmap and the run exercised the full-download path users are on today.

One caveat worth stating plainly: this proves the current published path works, it does not retroactively prove the blockmap was the original cause. The intent is right, but this removes the whole `<WindowTitlebar />` element rather than just the `onSidebarPreviewEnter` prop.

On Windows the window is frameless (`main.ts` sets `titleBarStyle: "hidden"`, `autoHideMenuBar: true`, plus `setMenuBarVisibility(false)`), so `WindowTitlebar` is the only thing painting the title bar. Dropping it means:

- no drag region at all: `.window-titlebar` (`styles.css:1332`) is the only `-webkit-app-region: drag` rule in the renderer, so the window cannot be moved by mouse
- File/Edit/View/Window/Help become mouse-unreachable, since the native menu bar is hidden and its replacement is gone
- `topbarOffset={isWindows ? "titlebar" : "toolbar"}` still reserves the 36px band, so it renders empty under the native window controls

CI stays green because the test file mocks `WindowTitlebar: () => null`, so nothing can catch it. The comment above the removed line is also still there, describing a component that no longer renders.

Suggested fix: keep `<WindowTitlebar />`, just drop the prop.

While you are in there, the peek machinery is now dead: `setIsSidebarPeekOpen(true)` is never called, so `isSidebarPeekOpen` is permanently false. That leaves the peek state and timer ref, `cancelSidebarPeekClose` / `scheduleSidebarPeekClose`, the global `pointermove` listener, `isOverlay` / `onPreviewLeave`, and the `onSidebarPreviewEnter` props on both `TitlebarNav` and `WindowTitlebar` with no way to trigger. @Vaibhaav-Tiwari happy to hop on a call if you'd still like, but let me try to explain it in writing first in case that's enough — it's a pretty small, self-contained bug once you see the root cause.

**What the user sees:** open a brand-new (untracked) file in the workspace diff viewer, and the synthetic diff shows one extra blank `+` line at the end that isn't really there, and the hunk header's line count (`@@ -0,0 +1,N @@`) is off by one from what the changed-files list shows for the same file.

**Where it comes from** — `syntheticAddedFileDiff` in `backend/internal/service/session/workspace_files.go` builds the diff by splitting the file's content on newlines:
```go
lines := strings.SplitAfter(content, "
")
```
`strings.SplitAfter` keeps the newline attached to each line, but it has a quirk: whenever the input ends with `
` (which is true for almost every text file), it produces one extra **empty string** as the final element. For example:
```go
strings.SplitAfter("hello
world
", "
")
// => ["hello
", "world
", ""]   <- 3 elements, but the file only has 2 lines!
```
The old code only handled the case where content was *completely* empty (`len(lines) == 1 && lines[0] == ""`), so that phantom trailing `""` survived for every normal file. The diff-building loop then does:
```go
for _, line := range lines {
    b.WriteByte('+')
    b.WriteString(line)
    ...
}
```
so that empty trailing element becomes a bare `+` with nothing after it — the extra blank line you see — and `len(lines)` (used for the `@@ -0,0 +1,N @@` header) is one too many.

**The fix:** instead of only special-casing the fully-empty-content case, always drop the split's trailing empty element when there is one:
```go
if n := len(lines); n > 0 && lines[n-1] == "" {
    lines = lines[:n-1]
}
```
This makes both the empty-file case and the completely normal "file ends with a newline" case behave correctly, and the line count now matches what `textLineCount` (used by the changed-files list) already reports — so the two views agree again.

I added a test (`workspace_files_test.go`) that covers: trailing newline, no trailing newline, single line, and empty content — and I verified by hand that it fails against the old code (reproducing the exact phantom `+` line) and passes with the fix.

Let me know if any part of that doesn't make sense, or if you'd still rather talk it through live — either works for me.

## Adversarial security + tenancy audit

I reviewed the PR head (`d6ae15a397fe7db87449f27b0ec7e89fa94dfe4a`), traced every Cloud HTTP/streaming route into the PostgreSQL stores, reviewed the worker/bootstrap/preview/provisioning paths, and compared this implementation with the failure classes from #3251.

### Critical

1. **Permanent coding-agent credentials and control-plane bearer material are delivered into the untrusted sandbox and inherited by arbitrary repository code**

   - `backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server.go:981-1056` decrypts the account's coding-agent credential and returns the plaintext secret in the unauthenticated bootstrap response.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/worker/client.go:23-40` models that plaintext as `AgentCredential.Secret` in the response.
   - `backend/cmd/ao-worker/main.go:43-53` reads the bootstrap token and exports the renewable worker token without unsetting the bootstrap token.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/worker/runner.go:123-168` builds the agent environment from `os.Environ()` plus the worker token and coding-agent secret.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/worker/runner.go:246-262` passes that same environment to both the agent PTY and the interactive workspace shell. Claude/Cursor secrets are explicitly placed in environment variables at `backend/internal/cloud/worker/runner.go:838-851`; Codex login writes a reusable credential under the persistent worker home at `backend/internal/cloud/worker/runner.go:853-875`.

   **Exploit scenario:** a malicious repository script, dependency, prompt-injected agent command, or user-supplied build step runs `env`/reads the persistent agent config and exfiltrates the coding-provider credential, `AO_WORKER_TOKEN`, and still-present `AO_WORKER_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN`. The provider credential is not session-scoped despite the type comment: it is the user's long-lived API/OAuth/access token. In an eventual organization model, one compromised sandbox would steal the shared organization credential. Printing it also enters the terminal stream and can persist in plaintext event payloads (`backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server.go:2051-2054`, `backend/internal/cloud/postgres/migrations/00001_cloud_foundation.sql:67-75`).

   **Required change:** do not inject permanent model/Git/provider credentials into an untrusted sandbox or workspace shell. Use a control-plane credential broker issuing provider-specific, narrowly scoped, short-lived grants (or a provider proxy), keep control tokens out of child environments, unset bootstrap material immediately, and add secret redaction before durable terminal/event persistence. This is a control-plane ownership blocker, not just hardening.

### High

2. **This is not the required multi-tenant organization model; it implements isolated single-user accounts**

   - `backend/internal/cloud/postgres/migrations/00001_cloud_foundation.sql:4-21` defines one unique `owner_user_id` per `ao_account`; projects and every downstream object are owned directly by that account. There are no organizations, memberships, roles, repository grants, or membership revocation/version facts.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server.go:280-293` maps each authenticated user directly to that sole account.
   - The PR's own design explicitly says the current schema is single-user ownership and "must replace" it with organization/membership/role/repository-grant ownership at `ao-cloud/architecture/CLOUD_DESIGN.md:88-95`.
   - Hosted mode still selects the local email/password authenticator (`backend/cmd/ao-cloud/main.go:54-56`; `ao-cloud/.env.hosted.example:16-17`) rather than the documented Clerk organization boundary.

   **Exploit/product scenario:** a team either cannot share a project at all, or must share one user's login/provider credentials. In the latter case every teammate is effectively owner, there is no request-time membership or role authorization, removing a teammate cannot revoke their access independently, and audit attribution is not trustworthy. A token for account A does appear unable to IDOR account B's current project/session routes, but that is per-user siloing, not the locked multi-tenant design.

   **Required change:** organization and personal-tenant records, memberships/roles, repository grants, tenant-owned credentials/audit/quota, and request-time membership authorization must be foundational schema/API work, not a later migration after product data exists.

3. **Worker bootstrap redemption is deliberately replayable and mints parallel, indefinitely renewable worker identities**

   - `backend/internal/cloud/postgres/store.go:1275-1290` accepts an already-consumed bootstrap ticket for two minutes.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server.go:1022-1056` re-registers the same worker ID/epoch, mints another worker bearer, and re-delivers launch data plus the plaintext agent credential on every replay.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server.go:1797-1802` lets any bearer for the current ID/epoch renew itself indefinitely through heartbeat.
   - The behavior is explicitly regression-tested at `backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server_integration_test.go:552-585` and `backend/internal/cloud/postgres/store_integration_test.go:370-399`.

   **Exploit scenario:** code in the sandbox inherits `AO_WORKER_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN`; it or an attacker receiving an exfiltrated copy replays within two minutes, obtains the coding-agent secret and a second current-epoch bearer, then heartbeats forever. Connecting the duplicate worker WebSocket at the same epoch replaces/closes the legitimate command stream (`backend/internal/cloud/workerhub/hub.go:46-66`), enabling durable worker impersonation and prompt/terminal interception. This repeats #3251's token-rotation concurrency class even though this PR calls the token a bootstrap ticket rather than a refresh token.

   **Required change:** atomically consume once. If retry after an ambiguous response is required, bind it to a server-side bootstrap transaction/channel and return a single already-issued result without creating multiple independently renewable credentials; rotate to a newer epoch on any replacement and revoke the prior one.

### Medium

4. **Account-controlled Daytona `apiUrl` is a stored SSRF primitive from the control-plane network**

   - `backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server.go:2816-2850` accepts an arbitrary `apiUrl`, performs only whitespace/trailing-slash normalization, then has the control plane validate it with a server-side request.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/sandbox/daytona/client.go:292-320` concatenates the supplied base URL with request paths and uses the default redirect-following HTTP client.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/sandboxresolve/resolver.go:78-90` reloads the stored URL and uses it for later lifecycle GET/POST/DELETE calls.

   **Exploit scenario:** any authenticated low-privilege account supplies an HTTP URL (or attacker redirector) targeting loopback, Compose-internal services, cloud metadata, or another trusted-network endpoint. Validation provides a timing/status/JSON oracle; subsequent provisioning causes trusted-network POST/DELETE traffic. I did not find a direct response-body exfiltration route, so I rank this medium rather than critical, but it is a real SSRF boundary.

   **Required change:** do not accept arbitrary provider base URLs in hosted mode. Pin Daytona origins, require HTTPS, disable or validate every redirect hop, resolve and reject loopback/private/link-local/reserved addresses (including DNS rebinding), and use an egress-restricted HTTP transport.

5. **Database tenant enforcement is fail-open: RLS is enabled but has no policies and the hosted app connects as the database owner/superuser**

   - `backend/internal/cloud/postgres/migrations/00001_cloud_foundation.sql:171-184` enables RLS but defines no policies and does not `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`.
   - `ao-cloud/docker-compose.hosted.yml:20-25,51-54` creates and connects as the same `POSTGRES_USER`; the initial PostgreSQL user is privileged and table owners bypass normal RLS.
   - Several tenant graph relationships are single-column foreign keys rather than `(account_id, id)` constraints. For example `ao_session_issue_links` can pair any session with any issue (`backend/internal/cloud/postgres/migrations/00007_cloud_orchestration.sql:18-21`), while `LinkSessionIssue` verifies the session account but not the issue account (`backend/internal/cloud/postgres/orchestration_store.go:49-55`). The current HTTP caller happens to pass an issue it just created in the same account, so I did not prove a present remote IDOR through this method.

   **Exploit scenario:** the next missed `account_id` predicate, store misuse, or injection is not stopped by PostgreSQL and can create/read cross-account rows. The comments currently imply a defense that is not active for the app role.

   **Required change:** use a non-owner least-privilege app role, transaction-local tenant context with real restrictive policies (and `FORCE RLS` where appropriate), and composite tenant keys/FKs for tenant-owned relationships. Keep application predicates too.

6. **Hosted password auth has no online-abuse controls**

   - Public signup/login are mounted outside auth at `backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server.go:165-170`.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/auth/local.go:75-106` performs database lookup + bcrypt and issues a 30-day opaque bearer, but has no per-account/source throttling, lockout, MFA, email verification, or session inventory/revoke-all.
   - `ao-cloud/Caddyfile:5-11` is only a reverse proxy; no edge rate policy is present.

   **Exploit scenario:** credential stuffing/password spraying can run without application or edge throttling, and a stolen bearer remains reusable for up to 30 days unless that exact token is explicitly logged out. This is materially below a public cloud control-plane auth baseline.

   **Required change:** ship the intended identity gateway/organization auth or add rate limiting, verified identities, MFA-capable sessions, short-lived access tokens with server-side revocation/session management, and security telemetry before public exposure.

### What is solid

- I did **not** find the #3251 arbitrary-user device approval bug: this PR has no device approval flow and does not accept a user ID to mint a browser session.
- Exposed project/session/event/turn/provider-connection store operations generally carry `account_id` and `session_id` predicates. Existing integration tests check cross-account session/message and credential isolation. I did not find an unscoped event replay fallback: REST SSE authorization is performed at `backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server.go:870-910`, replay queries are account/session-scoped, and live subscriptions key both account and session (`backend/internal/cloud/events/service.go:119-148`).
- Streaming auth is not REST-only: the worker WebSocket sits behind worker HMAC + current-epoch validation (`backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server.go:174-191,1062-1090`), and the browser terminal uses an atomically consumed, purpose-bound ticket plus an origin allowlist (`backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server.go:2283-2389`). Normal terminal tickets are one-use; the bootstrap exception is finding #3.
- Secrets are encrypted **before database persistence** with AES-GCM and account/provider/label associated data (`backend/internal/cloud/secrets/cipher.go:18-50`; `backend/internal/cloud/httpapi/server.go:2639-2654,2853-2868`). List/put responses omit ciphertext and request logging redacts preview-token paths. The critical issue is plaintext custody after decrypt/bootstrap, not at-rest encryption.
- SQL is parameterized. Docker commands use argv rather than a shell, Daytona shell values are quoted, workspace file inspection resolves symlinks and rejects escape (`backend/internal/cloud/worker/workspace_rpc.go:574-592`), localhost preview pins host/port through redirects, and the Git proxy checks the worker's exact project repository.
- #3251's JWT audience/OAuth-state bugs do not directly repeat because this PR does not implement JWT/OAuth at all. That also means the intended Clerk/org gateway is absent, as covered above.

### Verification

- `cd backend && go test ./internal/cloud/... ./cmd/ao-cloud ./cmd/ao-worker ./cmd/ao-cloud-agent` — passed.
- `cd backend && go test ./...` — not clean: non-cloud CLI/session tests failed in this AO session environment; the Cloud packages still passed.
- The focused landing-page Vitest command could not run because this checkout has no installed `vitest` binary. I did not install dependencies or modify the PR.

### Verdict

**Do not use #3426 as the cloud ownership/control-plane foundation in its current form.** The account-scoped query discipline and streaming ticket design are useful pieces, but the implementation is explicitly not organization multi-tenant, gives permanent credentials and renewable control authority to the untrusted execution plane, and intentionally permits bootstrap credential replay. Build ownership should not be handed over until credential brokerage and one-time worker identity are redesigned, organization/membership/repository authorization is made foundational, and the SSRF/database/sandbox boundaries fail closed.

## Correction: retracting the macOS "second reproduction" above

**This comment previously claimed a second independent reproduction on macOS and concluded the bug is not Windows-specific. That was wrong and I am retracting it.**

The macOS profile I cited burned versions 40 through 51 by running local `pipelines` feature branches, which define their own migrations in exactly that range:

```
0040_pipeline_tables.sql
0041_pr_is_from_fork.sql
0042_pr_cdc_update_head_sha.sql
0043_app_settings.sql
0044_pipeline_run_context.sql
0045_pipeline_run_blocks_merge.sql
0046_pipeline_stage_run_session_notes.sql
0047_pipelines_v2.sql
0048_session_pipeline_metadata.sql
0049_session_workspace_adopted.sql
0050_pipeline_stage_run_pgid.sql
0051_pipeline_run_number.sql
```

The apply timestamps line up with that branch work (40-43 on Jul 17, 44-46 on Jul 19, 47-49 on Jul 26, 50-51 on Jul 29). So that database is self-inflicted by running unmerged branches, and it is **not** evidence that released nightlies do this to ordinary users. It should not be used to argue scope, and it does not corroborate this report. Apologies for the noise on someone else's P1.

## What still stands

The mechanism is unchanged and is worth fixing regardless of how a version number gets burned:

- Once a version is recorded in `goose_db_version`, the real migration with that number is skipped silently.
- The failure then surfaces as an opaque 500 from a generated query referencing a column that was never created, with no migration error anywhere.
- `/healthz` and `/readyz` keep reporting healthy while the core workflow is dead, which actively misleads triage.

The fix requirements are also unchanged, and are what I would still argue for:

1. Forward repair migration numbered above any version plausibly burned, adding the columns only when absent, so it is safe on already-correct and hand-repaired databases alike.
2. Startup schema reconciliation that verifies the physical columns generated queries depend on, instead of trusting `goose_db_version` as the sole source of truth.
3. A guardrail rejecting reuse of a version number that has ever shipped.
4. Schema mismatches surfaced as a specific actionable error rather than `INTERNAL_ERROR`.

One caveat on point 1 that my retracted comment got right for the wrong reason: a repair that only checks whether the columns resolve will report a false all-clear on databases someone has already patched by hand. The repair needs to be idempotent, and triage should not treat a working `select diff_base_sha` as proof a profile was never affected.

## The open question this leaves, which is the important one

Upstream currently ships migrations only up to `0040`. So the question this report actually raises, and which my bad evidence obscured, is:

**How did a website-installed Windows nightly end up with versions 40 through 46 recorded on 2026-07-23?**

If that profile only ever ran released upstream nightlies, then a released build shipped migrations in that range and they were later renumbered or removed, which is a genuine upstream release problem and P1 is right. If that profile also ran a fork or branch build at some point, it is the same self-inflicted situation as my machine and the priority changes a lot.

That is worth confirming before anyone designs the fix, because it decides whether this needs a shipped repair migration for real users or just a guardrail plus documentation. I do not have visibility into that profile's install history.

## Correctness review (comment only, not an approval)

Thanks for the careful fail-closed design. The core unborn/broken-HEAD husk path looks right, and the preserve guard for non-husk dirs addresses the earlier deletion concern. I still see residual correctness gaps before this fully matches "init is atomic w.r.t. spawn eligibility."

### 1. Medium: valid HEAD does not mean checkout finished

`existingWorktree` / `Restore` / workspace-project recovery only treat a registered path as broken when `rev-parse HEAD` fails. Real git can leave a still-usable HEAD while checkout is incomplete.

Repro shape:

```bash
git worktree add --no-checkout -b feature /path/to/husk main
# dir often contains only .git
git -C /path/to/husk rev-parse --verify HEAD   # succeeds
git worktree lock --reason initializing /path/to/husk
```

On this PR, that registration is treated as ready and reused. If spawn is interrupted after HEAD is written but before checkout finishes (or in any equivalent "locked initializing + partial/empty tree + valid HEAD" state), AO can still hand a worker a non-usable tree. Issue #3220 is specifically unborn/broken HEAD, so that case is covered; the broader interrupted-init class is not.

Stronger options (pick one, with tests):

- Never reuse a worktree that is still `locked` with reason `initializing`, even when HEAD resolves. Only force-remove when `ensureInitializationHusk` passes; otherwise refuse.
- Or require unlocked + HEAD ok (and maybe a stronger readiness check) before reuse.

### 2. Medium: workspace-project new-branch path skips failed-attempt cleanup

In `createWorkspaceProjectRepo`:

- existing local branch path joins `cleanupFailedInitialization` on add failure
- the common `-b` / `addNewBranchWorktree` path does not

So a cancelled mid-add on the new-branch path can leave an initializing husk until a later call hits the pre-check recovery. Main `addWorktree` cleans both paths. Please route the `-b` failure path through the same cleanup helper (and cover it with a cancelled-context test like `TestAddWorktreeCleansInitializationCreatedByFailedAttempt`).

Also: when HEAD is already valid at `repo.outputPath`, the function still falls through to `worktree add` instead of returning success. That may be pre-existing for workspace projects, but the new HEAD check only handles the error branch, not "already ready."

### 3. Low: concurrent create on the same path

`cleanupFailedInitialization` with `registrationExisted == false` can force-remove another attempt's in-progress husk if two creates race the same path (A mid-init with only `.git`, B fails add and cleans). Session IDs usually unique the path, so this is unlikely in normal spawn, but it is still a check-then-delete race if double-create is possible.

### What looks good

- Parse `LockReason` from porcelain and key off exact `initializing`
- Refuse reuse when HEAD is bad and the worktree is not a proven init husk
- `ensureInitializationHusk` (only `.git` file) before unlock + force-remove
- `WithoutCancel` + timeout so cancelled spawn context still cleans attempt-owned husks on the main `addWorktree` path
- Real-git integration coverage for recover + preserve

### Suggested bar before merge

1. Do not treat `locked initializing` as reusable solely because HEAD resolves.
2. Wire failed-attempt cleanup into the workspace-project `-b` path with a test.
3. Keep the husk-only force-remove policy (that part is correct).

Not approving: the unborn-HEAD fix is in the right direction, but I would not call init atomic w.r.t. spawn eligibility yet.

## Correction — Original Root Cause Was Wrong

The original analysis claimed agy "silently drops" `SystemPrompt` because `GetLaunchCommand` / `GetAgentHooks` never reference it. **This is incorrect.**

As @nikhilachale pointed out: **Agy receives the system prompt through its SessionStart hook, not through launch arguments.** The delivery chain is:

1. **`prepareSystemPromptFile`** (`session_manager/manager.go:2603`) writes the system prompt to `$AO_DATA_DIR/prompts/<sessionID>/system.md` before launch.
2. `.gemini/hooks.json` (installed by `GetAgentHooks`) fires `ao hooks agy session-start` when the agy CLI starts.
3. **`runHook`** (`cli/hooks.go:148-150`) calls `shouldEmitSessionStartContext("agy", "session-start")` → `true`.
4. **`emitSessionStartContext`** (`cli/hooks.go:203-224`) reads `system.md` and emits it as `additionalContext` in the SessionStart hook JSON output — Gemini/Antigravity injects this into the conversation.

The system prompt IS delivered. A GEMINI.md-based fix (what I initially implemented) would **double-deliver** it and has been reverted.

---

## What's the actual bug?

@prateek's original report was "system prompt is not being appended properly." The hook-based delivery mechanism exists and appears structurally correct, so the bug is likely one of:

- **Timing:** `system.md` not written before the SessionStart hook fires
- **Environment:** `AO_SESSION_ID` or `AO_DATA_DIR` not set in the hook subprocess's environment
- **Hook output format mismatch:** agy/Gemini's expected `additionalContext` shape may have changed
- **Empty prompt:** the system prompt string itself is blank when it reaches `prepareSystemPromptFile`

**@prateek** — can you clarify the symptom? Is the system prompt partially delivered, truncated, or entirely absent? Do you see any errors in `~/.ao/hooks.log`?

## Not a Bug — Closing

Closing this issue. The original analysis was incorrect.

**Agy does receive the system prompt** — through its SessionStart hook, not through launch arguments. The delivery chain is:

1. `prepareSystemPromptFile` (`session_manager/manager.go:2603`) writes the system prompt to `$AO_DATA_DIR/prompts/<sessionID>/system.md` before launch.
2. `.gemini/hooks.json` fires `ao hooks agy session-start` when the agy CLI starts.
3. `runHook` (`cli/hooks.go:148-150`) calls `shouldEmitSessionStartContext("agy", "session-start")` → `true`.
4. `emitSessionStartContext` (`cli/hooks.go:203-224`) reads `system.md` and emits it as `additionalContext` in the SessionStart hook JSON output, which Gemini/Antigravity injects into the conversation.

The adapter never references `cfg.SystemPrompt` in `GetLaunchCommand` or `GetAgentHooks` directly — by design, not by omission. Flag-based adapters (Claude Code, Codex, Grok) pass it at launch; Agy (no system-prompt flag) receives it via the hook callback path instead.

Thanks to @nikhilachale for the correction.

## Correction after reproduction — original severity/cause was WRONG

A reproduction pass (electron-updater 6.8.9 + Electron 33.4.11, the shipped versions) overturns this issue's original framing. **Auto-update is NOT broken fleet-wide, and the org-rename redirect is NOT the cause of `net::ERR_FAILED`.**

Evidence (all reproduced locally):
1. Minimal electron-updater harness on the exact shipped versions, GitHub provider, nightly channel: check + asset download **succeed** against BOTH `owner=Untrivial-ai` and `owner=AgentWrapper` feeds — electron-updater follows the `301` (org rename) → `302` (release-assets.githubusercontent.com) chain cleanly.
2. The **real installed binary** (`v0.11.2-nightly.202608021445`, AgentWrapper-baked) run with an isolated HOME: it found `202608032052`, downloaded it fully through the AgentWrapper chain, and staged it via Squirrel with zero errors.
3. The reporter's own updater cache shows a **successful** auto-update to `202608021445` on Aug-2 (post-transfer) through the same chain.

**Actual cause of the reporter's `net::ERR_FAILED`:** a transient wedged Chromium network service in a long-running Electron instance (persists until process restart) — a per-instance issue, not a fleet outage. Confirmed pending an app restart.

## What IS real (the reason to keep this issue open, re-scoped)
Every build bakes `owner: AgentWrapper` (the pre-rename org): `build-artifacts.yml` never sets `AO_RELEASE_REPO`, so `frontend/forge.config.ts:10` falls back to the stale `DEFAULT_RELEASE_REPO`; the `ao-releases` conductor hardcodes AgentWrapper throughout. Updates currently work **only** via GitHub's org-transfer redirect, which would break **permanently** if the still-existing `AgentWrapper` account ever creates a repo named `agent-orchestrator`.

**Severity: high (latent), not critical (active). No mass reinstall required** — the fleet self-heals through a normal nightly once the pipeline bakes the correct owner.

## Fix (unchanged in substance)
1. Bake `Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator`: fix the forge default + set `AO_RELEASE_REPO` in `build-artifacts.yml` + `feature-builds.ts` DEFAULT_REPO; AgentWrapper→Untrivial-ai throughout `ao-releases`.
2. Regression guard: extend `macOS update e2e` to assert the bundled `app-update.yml` owner matches the publishing repo AND follows the real feed redirect chain end-to-end.
3. (Separate) the transient wedged-network `net::ERR_FAILED` is worth its own hardening ticket if it recurs, but is not this issue.

Hi @anmol0b — thanks for working on this. I traced the current PR head against #3327 and the existing Windows lifecycle code. Could you please check whether the concerns below actually apply on Windows? I may be missing Windows-specific behavior, so I am framing these as verification questions rather than conclusions.

### 1. Does `taskkill /T` unintentionally kill sessions that are meant to survive daemon restart?

The process relationship appears to be:

```text
Electron -> daemon -> detached pty-host -> agent
```

`killDaemon()` now runs `taskkill /pid <daemon-pid> /T /F`. Microsoft documents `/T` as ending the target and its child processes: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/taskkill

However, `spawn_windows.go` deliberately creates each pty-host with `DETACHED_PROCESS | CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` so it survives daemon exit, and backend shutdown deliberately omits session teardown so the next daemon can adopt those sessions:

- https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/1b675d646d3d37625e2bf95515711bcc47eeeb2e/backend/internal/adapters/runtime/conpty/spawn_windows.go#L89-L100
- https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/1b675d646d3d37625e2bf95515711bcc47eeeb2e/backend/internal/daemon/lifecycle_wiring.go#L111-L118

`DETACHED_PROCESS` changes console inheritance, and `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` changes control-event grouping; neither appears to remove the daemon/child ancestry used by `taskkill /T`. Could you please verify on Windows whether explicit daemon stop/restart and the disconnected-supervisor exit fallback now terminate all active pty-hosts/agents? If they do, this conflicts with the current session-survival contract and may need a daemon-only termination strategy instead of recursive tree kill.

### 2. Do the new `taskkill` branches run for the reported close/Task Manager paths?

For a normal connected app quit, the exit handler explicitly skips `killDaemon()` when `supervisorLink.connected` is true:

https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/1b675d646d3d37625e2bf95515711bcc47eeeb2e/frontend/src/main.ts#L1574-L1588

A forced Task Manager termination also cannot be expected to run Node's JavaScript `process.on("exit")` callback; Node documents that event for `process.exit()` and an exhausted event loop: https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#event-exit

The existing supervisor socket may still stop the daemon after either exit, so I am **not** asserting that the daemon definitely remains alive. The concern is that this supervisor behavior predates the PR and deliberately leaves ConPTY sessions alive, whereas #3327 expects closing AO to stop “daemon, workers, and all child processes.” Could you please reproduce the original normal-close and Task Manager symptoms on a real Windows machine and confirm which path fixes them, including the reported app reopening?

### 3. Is the changed PID probe involved in ordinary UI worker termination?

The normal UI path appears to be:

```text
POST /sessions/{id}/kill
  -> session Manager.Kill
  -> ConPTY Runtime.Destroy
  -> conpty.pidAlive
  -> ptyregistry.Unregister
```

`conpty.pidAlive` already delegated to `processalive.Alive` at this PR's base; that fix merged in #3082 before this branch. This PR changes the separate `ptyregistry.defaultPidAlive`, which is used when `Runtime.resolve` falls back to registry recovery because the session is absent from memory.

- Existing runtime probe: https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/1b675d646d3d37625e2bf95515711bcc47eeeb2e/backend/internal/adapters/runtime/conpty/pidalive_windows.go#L12-L15
- Destroy path: https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/1b675d646d3d37625e2bf95515711bcc47eeeb2e/backend/internal/adapters/runtime/conpty/runtime.go#L107-L140
- Registry fallback: https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/1b675d646d3d37625e2bf95515711bcc47eeeb2e/backend/internal/adapters/runtime/conpty/runtime.go#L213-L244
- Earlier fix: #3082

Could you please confirm that stale registry recovery is actually part of the reported respawn sequence? Otherwise the registry change appears to fix a valid but different stale-entry bug, while the normal UI-kill behavior in #3327 remains unchanged.

### 4. Verification/tests

The PR adds no direct tests for the real Windows PID probe or either destructive `taskkill` boundary; existing registry tests replace `pidAlive` with a fake. Could we add an actual Windows liveness regression test and an injected/testable process-termination seam covering command arguments, failure handling, and session survival? The duplicated `taskkill` blocks could then share that helper.

Also, GitHub currently marks the PR as conflicting with `main`, so it will need a rebase/update after these checks.

Please let me know if any call-path or Windows-process assumption above is wrong; happy to re-check it against concrete reproduction results.

Implemented terminal replay and resize stability fixes:

- Split large first-open terminal replay into 256 KB `xterm.write()` batches to reduce long renderer-blocking tasks.
- Preserve exact PTY output order when live data arrives during replay.
- Safely drain pending replay data before terminal exit or reconnect.
- Wait for fullscreen/layout transitions to settle before fitting xterm.
- Remove duplicate fits and unconditional full-grid refreshes.
- Ignore unchanged terminal dimensions in both Electron and the daemon.
- Prevent secondary viewers from redundantly resizing a shared PTY.
- Fall back to Canvas when the WebGL context is lost.

These changes reduce visible first-open repainting, unnecessary TUI redraws, and renderer stalls. Large or continuously streaming terminals may still show a CPU spike because xterm must parse and render the complete output; batching improves responsiveness but does not eliminate the total parsing cost.

## Это не первый раз — команда сносит всё подряд, без разбора

Важное дополнение к описанию выше: случай, приведённый в issue, **не разовый**. По словам пользователя, `ao session cleanup` регулярно удаляет всё подряд, безотносительно того, что это за workspace и нужен ли он ещё. Приведённый инцидент — просто тот, который удалось задокументировать пошагово с выводом команд.

Это меняет характер проблемы. Речь не о частном промахе фильтра для оркестраторских сессий, а о том, что **у команды по факту нет надёжного критерия «что можно удалять»**. Она ведёт себя как «снести всё в каталоге проекта», а обещает при этом «reclaim eligible workspaces of terminated sessions».

### Почему это больно

`cleanup` — команда обслуживания. Её запускают рутинно, чтобы освободить место, и по названию ожидают консервативного поведения. Вместо этого она:

- удаляет workspace живой сессии (`terminated: false`, `status: working`) — задокументировано выше;
- удаляет workspace той самой сессии, из которой её вызвали;
- делает это, не показав удаляемое в `--dry-run` (превью перечислило 178 сессий, среди которых удалённого оркестраторского workspace **не было**).

Последний пункт — самый неприятный: `--dry-run` существует ровно для того, чтобы можно было посмотреть перед выполнением. Если фактический эффект шире превью, то превью не защищает, и осторожность пользователя ничего не даёт.

### Чего хотелось бы

1. **Явный, документированный критерий удаления** — и чтобы фактическое поведение ему соответствовало. Если удаляется что-то, кроме workspace терминированных сессий, это должно быть либо убрано, либо явно описано и показано в превью.
2. **`--dry-run` = полный перечень того, что реально исчезнет.** Без исключений и «дополнительных зачисток» помимо списка.
3. **Безусловная защита живых сессий и текущей сессии**, независимо от роли (worker/orchestrator) и от того, попала ли сессия в перечень.
4. **Отказ по умолчанию для грязных worktree** — если в каталоге есть незакоммиченные изменения, не удалять без отдельного явного флага. (В описании команды упоминается, что «dirty worktrees are skipped by the daemon» — стоит проверить, действительно ли это работает на всех путях удаления, включая тот, что снёс оркестраторский workspace мимо dry-run-списка.)

Пока это не починено, команду опасно запускать без предварительной ручной проверки, что сводит на нет её смысл как рутинного обслуживания.

## Correcting my own earlier root-cause comment — the model is never sent on restore

My 2026-07-28 comment above says the stored model is derived on both paths and "forwarded unchanged to the agent CLI's `--model` flag". The first half is right; **the second half is wrong**, and the distinction turns out to be the whole bug. I traced it properly against `c700e29dc`.

### The manager resolves and passes it. The adapter drops it.

`backend/internal/session_manager/manager.go:1038` resolves the config on restore, under a comment that states the intended property outright:

```go
// Restore re-applies the project's resolved agent config so a configured
// model/permissions carry across a restore, matching fresh spawn.
agentConfig := effectiveAgentConfig(rec.Kind, project.Config)
```

and `manager.go:2785` passes it through:

```go
cmd, ok, err := agent.GetRestoreCommand(ctx, ports.RestoreConfig{..., Config: agentConfig, Permissions: agentConfig.Permissions})
```

`ports.RestoreConfig` (`backend/internal/ports/agent.go:246`) carries `Config AgentConfig`. So the model is present at the adapter's call site.

But in `backend/internal/adapters/agent/claudecode/claudecode.go`:

- the **start** path (line 172) does `if model := strings.TrimSpace(cfg.Config.Model); model != "" { cmd = append(cmd, "--model", model) }`
- `GetRestoreCommand` (line 227) builds `binary → permission flags → --append-system-prompt → --resume <id>` and **never reads `cfg.Config.Model`**

So the resume argv carries no model at all. The CLI then resolves from its own defaults — including tier-keyed environment defaults such as `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL` when they are set in the daemon's environment.

**That reframes this issue.** The reported MiniMax-M3 → `claude-fable-5` substitution is not the CLI rejecting an unrecognized model string and falling back. The CLI was never given a model string on the resume command line, so it did what it is supposed to do with no `--model`: use its default. There is nothing for a validation or allow-list change to fix, because no value reaches the validator.

### Why the comment at `manager.go:1038` is what hid this

That comment asserts "model/permissions carry across a restore". Permissions genuinely do — `GetRestoreCommand` calls `appendPermissionFlags(&cmd, cfg.Permissions)` and its doc comment explains why ("resume otherwise reverts to the configured default"). The identical argument applies to the model and was never made. Half the stated property holds, which reads as the whole property holding.

### It is not one adapter

There are **23 hand-rolled `GetRestoreCommand` implementations**. Scanning each function body for any reference to `Model`:

- **12 contain none at all**: `agentbase`, `agy`, `amp`, `claudecode`, `continueagent`, `crush`, `cursor`, `devin`, `droid`, `grok`, `kiro`, `opencode`
- 11 reference it — but at least one of those is a false positive in the safe direction: `copilot` (`copilot.go:154`) deliberately does **not** forward the model on resume, with a documented reason (`--model` + `--resume` interoperation unverified). So 12 is a lower bound.

A blanket "append `--model` in every restore builder" would therefore regress `copilot`'s deliberate choice.

### Suggested shape

Rather than patching `claudecode`:

1. resolve start and restore argv through **one launch-config assembly seam**, so restore cannot omit what start applies;
2. give adapters an **explicit, typed opt-out** for "does not forward model on resume", so `copilot`'s decision is declared rather than indistinguishable from an omission;
3. add a **table-driven test over all registered adapters** asserting each either forwards the model on resume or carries that opt-out. Silence must not mean omitted — that is precisely the state that produced this bug.

Points 1 and 3 are what stop this recurring the next time an adapter is added.

### Related

The blast radius runs in both directions: a session provisioned on a cheap model resumes on the user's default (a cost leak), and a session provisioned on a large-context model resumes on a smaller one (which we hit at scale after a daemon restart — every restored orchestrator silently lost its configured context window, with the config still reading correctly).

Happy to open a PR for the seam + parity test if that shape is agreeable, or to leave it if a maintainer would rather land it differently.

The original prevention fix in PR #3262 is present on current `main`, and its focused tests pass. However, the user-visible problem survives an update because the fix only gates **new discovery**; it never validates or detaches PR rows that were already attributed incorrectly.

### Local evidence

- Analyzed checkout: `ae0541324` (`origin/main`).
- Current desktop: `0.12.1-nightly.202608051954`; daemon is healthy on port 3001.

### Code-path gap

`discoverNewPRs` applies the authenticated-author gate only before inserting an untracked PR. Once a PR exists in `subjects`/storage, subsequent polls refresh it without rechecking ownership. PR #3262 did not add startup/poll reconciliation or an explicit detach path for invalid historical auto-attributions.

### Recommended scope

1. Track attachment provenance (`automatic` vs explicit `claim-pr`/review claim), so reconciliation never undoes an intentional claim.
2. Revalidate automatically discovered PRs when a human SCM identity is known; detach/quarantine foreign-author rows that only match by branch namespace.
3. Fail closed for *new automatic attribution* when identity lookup fails, while keeping explicit `claim-pr` as the override. The current fallback deliberately restores the original unsafe behavior during transient identity failures.
4. Add an end-to-end regression test covering: bad row created under the old behavior -> daemon starts with known identity -> row is no longer attached; explicit foreign-author claim remains attached.

**Confidence:** High for the missing-remediation gap; Medium for any post-fix new-attribution regression (the observed rows predate the currently installed build).

## New reproduction: PR shows 2 files, AO shows 36

**Reported by:** @illegalcall in Codex chat (screenshots below)  
**Date:** 2026-08-07  
**Affected session:** `agent-orchestrator-1-55` (`fix-chat-jump-bg`)  
**Source PR:** [PR #3680](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/3680)  
**Analyzed against:** `f17013b53a1752e86c66e87b45aaa4a463fdff62` (`origin/main`)  
**AO version:** `dev`, verified Go daemon on `127.0.0.1:3001`  
**Confidence:** High — reproduced from the live endpoint and traced to the exact comparison branch.

![Summary showing PR #3680 has 2 files while the inspector tab says 36 Files](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issue-assets-3203-pr-file-count-20260807/.issue-assets/pr-file-count/workspace-summary.png)

![Files tab showing unrelated changes included in the session diff](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issue-assets-3203-pr-file-count-20260807/.issue-assets/pr-file-count/workspace-files.png)

### Reproduction

1. Spawn a session from `main` at commit `ca75b9c34de650cc67951ad7feecd6f6f0b77b4e`.
2. Commit a two-file session change (`19cf54cff8b9bbcb4d8929a409406bdcb9995859`).
3. Let `main` advance independently to `f17013b53a1752e86c66e87b45aaa4a463fdff62`.
4. Open [PR #3680](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/3680), then inspect the session's Files tab.

GitHub correctly reports these 2 files:

- `frontend/src/renderer/components/chat/ChatWorkspace.test.tsx`
- `frontend/src/renderer/components/chat/ChatWorkspace.tsx`

The live AO endpoint returned `compareBaseSha=f17013b...`, `compareBaseRef=main`, and 36 changed files:

```text
HEAD:       19cf54cff (parent ca75b9c34)
PR base:    f17013b53
merge-base: ca75b9c34

git diff --name-only f17013b53 HEAD        => 36 files
git diff --name-only $(git merge-base ...) HEAD => 2 files
```

The extra 34 entries are base-only changes rendered in reverse (for example deleted landing assets and reverted daemon/UI edits). The worktree itself is clean.

### Root cause

This is an incomplete fallback in the fix from [PR #3214](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/3214), not a frontend count bug.

For this observed session, `sessions.diff_base_sha` and `sessions.diff_base_ref` are empty. The daemon therefore reaches the PR fallback in [`resolveWorkspaceCompare`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/f17013b53a1752e86c66e87b45aaa4a463fdff62/backend/internal/service/session/workspace_files.go#L278-L282). That branch returns the provider's current `pr.BaseSHA` directly after only checking that the commit exists. It does **not** compute `git merge-base HEAD <pr.BaseSHA>`.

The downstream status and numstat paths then run a two-endpoint tree comparison against that raw SHA ([`workspaceDiffStatuses`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/f17013b53a1752e86c66e87b45aaa4a463fdff62/backend/internal/service/session/workspace_files.go#L1005-L1007), [`workspaceNumstat`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/f17013b53a1752e86c66e87b45aaa4a463fdff62/backend/internal/service/session/workspace_files.go#L1075-L1077)). When the PR base branch has advanced since the worker forked, that comparison includes both the worker's changes and the inverse of every base-only change.

The renderer is behaving consistently with the bad daemon response: [`useSessionWorkspaceFilesChangedCount`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/f17013b53a1752e86c66e87b45aaa4a463fdff62/frontend/src/renderer/hooks/useSessionWorkspaceFiles.ts#L35-L50) counts every file whose returned status is not `unmodified`.

The existing `TestWorkspaceFilesPRFallbackPrefersDefaultTargetPR` does not catch this because its PR `BaseSHA` is also the branch point; the base never advances independently.

### Suggested fix

- In the PR fallback, resolve the merge base of `HEAD` and `pr.BaseSHA`; expose that merge-base SHA as `CompareBaseSHA` while retaining the PR target branch as `CompareBaseRef`.
- Add a regression where the worker and target branch diverge after the worker is created and the session has no recorded diff base. Assert that base-only files remain `unmodified` and only worker-side files are counted/returned as changed.
- Apply the same resolved target to file status, numstat, and per-file patches.

### Impact / priority

**P2:** the Files tab and review surface can substantially misrepresent a small PR and distract reviewers with unrelated or reversed changes. GitHub's PR Files view is a workaround and remains correct.
